format: Each lesson has five formative questions (error, guided1, guided2, independent1, independent2) and two different required-check questions. Each row is prompt, correct option, three distractors, then explanatory feedback.

01: A learner says the warm room itself infected everyone who ate a lunch. Which correction is strongest?
Warmth can favour growth if a pathogen was present; exposure to the pathogen still needs evidence.
Warm conditions alone are sufficient to introduce a pathogen into uncontaminated food.
Temperature alone identifies the exact bacterium.
An inherited condition is established solely by the timing of illness after this meal.
Distinguish a condition that changes growth from the agent and exposure that could cause infection.
Which observation would best begin testing a foodborne explanation?
Compare what affected and unaffected people ate and when symptoms began.
Ask only whether the room looked clean.
Compare package appearance without checking what affected and unaffected people actually ate.
Assume everyone at the school had the same exposure.
A comparison across cases and exposures tests the claim better than appearance or assumption.
Why might a hamburger left warm become riskier over time?
Some bacteria already present may reproduce under suitable conditions.
Warmth by itself introduces a new pathogen into otherwise uncontaminated food.
Warmth guarantees every eater will become sick.
Chilling slows growth but by itself removes every microbe already present.
Growth requires an organism and suitable conditions; risk is not a guaranteed outcome.
A student lists poverty as a pathogen. What is the reasoning error?
A social condition can alter exposure and access to care but is not itself an infectious agent.
Social conditions can never affect health.
Every disease linked to poverty is inherited.
A pathogen is just another word for any risk factor.
Keep an infectious agent distinct from conditions that shape risk and response.
Two people ate the same meal; one became ill. What is a defensible conclusion?
Investigate agent, dose, other exposures and host factors before assigning a cause.
The different outcomes prove one person handled the food incorrectly.
The meal is proven safe because one person stayed well.
The room temperature alone proves a diagnosis.
Different outcomes do not establish or exclude a food source without more evidence.
What would make a germ claim stronger than a guess?
Consistent evidence linking a specified organism, exposure and cases while checking alternatives.
A single vivid story without comparisons.
The fact that all microbes are harmful.
A label that calls any warm food contaminated.
Germ theory is tested with specific evidence, comparisons and alternative explanations.
Which statement best separates cause and contributing condition in a food-illness case?
A pathogen may cause infection; warm storage may increase its amount if it is present.
Warm storage is the pathogen and the bacterium is the temperature.
If a food looks normal no pathogen can be present.
A risk factor proves a particular person's diagnosis.
The agent and the conditions that affect exposure or growth play different roles.
02: A learner says a cold virus divides by itself on a sandwich like a bacterial cell. What is the error?
A virus needs a suitable host cell to make more virus particles.
Bacteria never reproduce in food.
Viruses and fungi are the same type of cellular organism.
A virus can multiply on food without entering a host cell.
Bacteria are cells that may divide independently; viruses use host cells for replication.
Which pair is correctly matched in the workbook examples?
Giardia — protist; athlete's foot — fungus.
Giardia — virus; athlete's foot — bacterium.
Giardia — fungus; athlete's foot — protist.
Both are bacterial diseases with the same exposure route.
The examples involve different groups and need different transmission explanations.
Which route could explain Giardia exposure in a hiking case?
Swallowing contaminated untreated water.
Knowing that beavers can carry Giardia without a water-exposure pathway.
Being outdoors without evidence of a contaminated water source.
Having a naturally occurring DNA allele.
The waterborne route connects an environmental source with entry into the digestive system.
An antibiotic helped one infection, so a learner wants it for every viral cold. Which response uses mechanism?
Antibiotics target bacteria; they do not directly act on a cold virus.
Fever is enough to classify this infection as bacterial.
Viral particles split independently like bacteria.
A medicine that helped once must work for every cause.
Treatment depends on the agent and clinical context, not the general word 'infection'.
A rash is described as definitely fungal from appearance alone. What is missing?
Evidence distinguishing fungal infection from other infectious and non-infectious causes.
A complete list of all nearby microbes, regardless of exposure route.
Proof that all skin rashes are contagious.
A claim that fungi are viruses.
A symptom can suggest possibilities but does not identify the agent by itself.
Which comparison of bacteria and viruses is accurate?
Bacteria are cells; viruses require host-cell machinery to replicate.
Viruses are cells that divide by binary fission in food.
Bacteria have no cellular structure.
Both are identical in size, reproduction and treatment.
The distinction concerns cellular organization and reproduction, not merely whether illness occurs.
A water sample may contain a protist. Which conclusion follows?
A particular disease claim needs identification and exposure evidence, since not all protists are pathogens.
Every protist in water causes beaver fever.
Only beavers can carry a waterborne pathogen.
The sample proves every hiker is infected.
Category, pathogenicity and actual exposure are separate pieces of evidence.
03: A learner calls crowded housing a pathogen. Which correction is best?
It can increase contact and exposure opportunities; a pathogen is the disease-causing agent.
It can never influence transmission.
It is a kind of virus.
It proves every resident has an infection.
Separate a social condition from the microorganism and transmission route.
Which condition is communicable in the relevant sense?
An infection that can pass between hosts through a route.
A chromosome-number pattern inherited through reproduction.
A broken bone from a fall.
A nutritional deficiency with no infectious agent.
Communicable describes spread of an infectious condition between hosts.
Which question helps compare two old mortality charts fairly?
Do they use the same date, population, age range and measure?
Compare bar colours without checking the legend, date or denominator.
Compare the place names rather than the rates and time periods.
Can a dated number be called today's rate?
Time, denominator and measurement type determine whether a comparison is meaningful.
A student says poor water access means residents are biologically more likely to be infected. What is the error?
Unequal water infrastructure changes exposure; it does not define inherent biology of residents.
Water cannot carry infectious agents.
Inherited factors alone determine whether a person becomes infected.
Public systems cannot reduce exposure.
The mechanism is exposure through a system, not a trait assigned to a group.
Two diseases both harm health, but only one spreads by contact. What should the classification use?
The demonstrated transmission mechanism, not just severity or symptom.
Use the larger raw case count without adjusting for population size.
Whether someone is worried about it.
Use an undated number without checking how or when it was measured.
Communicability is about spread between hosts; severity is another dimension.
Which statement uses a historical life-expectancy chart responsibly?
It reports the chart's period and measure, then seeks newer data for a current claim.
It applies the old ranking to all people today.
It treats income as a pathogen.
It ignores differences in data collection.
Historical data support claims about their time and method, not an eternal ranking.
A class compares disease risk between communities. What is the strongest explanation?
Name the agent and route, then examine exposure, infrastructure and access separately.
Assign the difference to one group's worth.
Treat risk factors as proof of each person's diagnosis.
Ignore the denominator and time period.
A mechanistic, contextual explanation avoids both biological and statistical overreach.
04: A student says refrigeration sterilizes food. Which correction is best?
Cold slows many microbes; it does not reliably eliminate every pathogen.
Cold creates new pathogens.
Refrigeration is identical to pasteurization.
Food safety depends only on colour.
Preservation methods change conditions or reduce hazards in different ways; cold storage is not sterilization.
Which method primarily reduces available water for microbial growth?
Drying or salting.
Leaving food on a warm counter.
Using the same unwashed board for raw and ready-to-eat food.
Removing the product label.
Less available water can limit microbial growth in a specific preservation method.
Why does pasteurization not mean opened milk may stay warm indefinitely?
It reduces targeted microbes through controlled heat but later contamination and growth remain possible.
It makes milk completely sterile, so later storage and handling cannot matter.
It works only by freezing the product.
It protects milk by adding a vaccine rather than by controlled heat treatment.
Controlled processing has limits; safe storage after opening still matters.
A salad is prepared on a board used for raw poultry. Which intervention addresses the route?
Use separate or properly cleaned and sanitized equipment before the salad is prepared.
Only chill the salad after contamination.
Assume vegetables kill microbes from poultry.
Wait until the board looks dry without cleaning it.
Cross-contamination occurs during transfer from the raw-food surface to ready-to-eat food.
Which statement about freezing is defensible?
It slows or stops growth while frozen but cannot be assumed to sterilize the food.
It makes all food safe forever.
It guarantees every microbe is destroyed.
It increases room-temperature bacterial division.
Freezing changes growth conditions; organisms may survive and grow after thawing.
Why do clean preparation surfaces and cold storage both matter?
They interrupt different points: transfer of microbes and later growth conditions.
They are the same chemical procedure.
Either one guarantees all hazards disappear.
Only storage matters after raw food touches salad.
Layered controls address different mechanisms and limitations.
A learner writes 'every preservation method kills germs.' What is a stronger summary?
Methods such as drying, chilling and heat processing act through different mechanisms and have different limits.
All ten workbook methods are identical.
No method changes risk.
A method's name proves all foods are sterile.
Mechanism-based explanations are needed for the workbook's ten named methods.
05: A learner puts hard-surface disinfectant on a cut because it 'kills germs.' What is the error?
A product for surfaces is not interchangeable with a skin antiseptic; follow the intended-use label.
Skin and countertops are the same material.
Antiseptic means a stronger floor cleaner.
All disinfectants are safe on living tissue.
Microbial action and tissue safety are separate requirements.
What best describes sterilization?
A validated process intended to eliminate all viable microorganisms from an item.
Any visible wipe of a table.
Keeping an item in a refrigerator.
Applying hand lotion.
Sterilization has a more demanding outcome than ordinary cleaning or disinfection.
A prepared tool touches an unclean counter. What changed?
It may have become contaminated despite earlier preparation.
It became automatically more sterile.
The counter no longer contains any microbes.
Gloves alone replace surface preparation and sterile equipment.
Aseptic practice must prevent re-contamination throughout the procedure.
Which method is intended for suitable non-living surfaces?
A disinfectant used according to its label.
Use a skin antiseptic on an instrument without checking whether it can sterilize the instrument.
An antiseptic chosen without label review.
Cooling instruments is enough to make them sterile.
Disinfectants and antiseptics differ in intended target and safe use.
Why is hand cleaning alone insufficient after sterile equipment is put on a dirty surface?
The equipment should be treated as potentially contaminated before continuing.
Hands can never transfer microbes.
Aseptic technique only happens before the task.
The original cleaning step makes later contact irrelevant.
Each new contact can break the chain of controls.
Which pair correctly matches method and target?
Antiseptic—living tissue; disinfectant—suitable non-living surface.
Disinfectant—any open wound; antiseptic—every floor.
Sterilization—ordinary refrigeration; asepsis—a chemical bottle.
Antibiotic—sterilize a workbench; vaccine—clean a cut.
Terms identify intended use and process, not interchangeable levels of strength.
A student lists four aseptic steps. What makes the explanation complete?
Each step names the contamination route it prevents and stays within trained procedures.
The four steps are interchangeable because they interrupt the same route.
The list assumes gloves make every surface sterile.
The steps invite an unsupervised procedure at home.
The source task calls for practices tied to mechanisms, with practical work under supervision.
